Are there infinitely many $n$ such that $\binom{2n}{n}$ is coprime to $105$?
#376: [ErGr80,p.71]
number theory | 
binomial coefficients | 
base representations
Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus [EGRS75] have shown that, for any two odd primes $p$ and $q$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\binom{2n}{n}$ is coprime to $pq$. 
This is equivalent (via Kummer's theorem) to whether there are infinitely many $n$ which have only digits $0,1$ in base $3$, digits $0,1,2$ in base $5$, and digits $0,1,2,3$ in base $7$.
The sequence of such $n$ is A030979 in the OEIS.
The best result in this direction is due to Bloom and Croot [BlCr25], who proved that, if $p_1,p_2,p_3$ are sufficiently large primes, then there are infinitely many $n$ such that almost all of the base $p_i$ digits are $<p_i/2$. In other words, for all $\epsilon>0$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\binom{2n}{n}$ is coprime to $p_1p_2p_3$, except for a factor of size $\leq n^\epsilon$.
This is mentioned in problem B33 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. It is also discussed in an article of Pomerance [Po15c]. 
Graham offered \$1000 for a solution to this problem (as mentioned in [Gu04] and [BeHa98]).

 There is recent work in the direction of this problem at
Croot, Ernie; Mousavi, Hamed; Schmidt, Maxie, On a conjecture of Graham on the p-divisibility of central binomial coefficients
Mathematika 70, No. 3, Article ID e12249, 29 p. (2024). 
They construct $n$ for which $\binom{2n}{n}$ is divisible by an unusually small number of powers of $p$ for any fixed set of small primes $p$ (e.g., $p=3,5,7$), although they cannot get this number down to zero (which is what is needed for this problem).
EDIT: I see now that the already cited paper [BlCr2025] mentions this previous work and improves upon it.

 Yes, apologies I should have also cited the Croot, Mousavi, and Schmidt paper (which my paper with Croot improves). For reference, here is what the two papers say in terms of this problem. 
Given a finite set of primes $P=\{p_1<\cdots<p_k\}$ let $f_P(n)$ be the $P$-divisible component of $\binom{2n}{n}$ (that is, the product of all maximal powers of $p_i\in P$ which divide $\binom{2n}{n}$). It is trivial that $f_P(n) \leq n^{O(k)}$. 
Croot, Mousavi, and Schmidt proved that, for any $\epsilon>0$, if $p_1$ is sufficiently large depending on $\epsilon$ and $k$, then there are infinitely many $n$ such that $f_P(n)\leq n^\epsilon$.
Croot and I in [BlCr25] proved that, provided $p_1$ is sufficiently large depending only on $k$ (e.g. $\geq 10^{94}$ for $k=3$) then, for any $\epsilon>0$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $f_P(n) \leq n^\epsilon$.
So essentially we swapped the quantifiers round so that $\epsilon$ is now independent of the set of primes. We believe that a more careful version of our proof should allow one to prove that, if $p_1$ is large enough in terms of $k$, then there are infinitely many $n$ such that $f_p(n) \leq \exp(O(\sqrt{\log n}))$. 
(Of course the conjecture is that, generalising the problem of Graham mentioned here, that if $p_1$ is sufficiently large in terms of $k$ then $f_P(n)=1$ for infinitely many $n$.)
